The conditions

April. The Romanian edition of the novel has come off the press. The launch will take place at the Instituto Cervantes in Bucharest, and Marta has promised to come. Costel comes to the B2 class with a proposal.
I have an idea. In May I have a trip to Portugal with the lorry. I can take the Romanian books to the Madrid fair.
And will your boss let you?
As long as the books don’t weigh more than a hundred kilos, yes. And provided I bring him a signed copy.
I’ll sign as many as you like, on condition that you arrive before the thirtieth of May.
I’ll arrive on the twenty-eighth, unless there’s a strike at the French border.
And Andrés? What did the doctor say?
That he can go to the fair provided it isn’t hot and he doesn’t stay there more than an hour. Unless he gets worse, of course.
In case it’s hot, the launch could be in the morning.
I’ve already suggested that to the fair’s director. If I’d known earlier, I would have asked for it from the start.
Well, that’s settled. But I’m warning you: if you don’t keep me a seat in the front row, I’m going back to Bucharest with all the books.
(laughing) We’ll keep you the best seat, Costel. Unless you’re late.

Said as a single group: [kon-tal-de-que]. The main stress falls on the verb that follows.
«¡Como no vengas…!» is said with a rising, emphatic tone, like a half-joking threat.
e-jem-PLAR: strongly aspirated “j”, stress on the last syllable.
1. Necessary condition: siempre que, con tal de que, a condición de que
They all take the SUBJUNCTIVE when they refer to the present or future:
He’ll be able to go provided it isn’t hot.
I’ll take the books for you as long as you invite me.
I’ll sign them for you on condition that you arrive on time.
“Siempre que” + INDICATIVE means “every time”: «Siempre que viene, trae flores» (Every time she comes, she brings flowers). + SUBJUNCTIVE = condition: «siempre que venga» (provided she comes).
2. The exception: a no ser que, a menos que, salvo que
They introduce the only situation in which the consequence does NOT happen. They all take the SUBJUNCTIVE:
I’ll arrive on the twenty-eighth, unless there’s a strike.
We’ll keep your seat, unless you’re late.
He’ll go to the fair, unless he gets worse.
Watch the meaning: “a no ser que” already contains the negation. «A no ser que llueva» = “unless it rains”, not “if it rains”.
3. En caso de que, por si, de + infinitive
En caso de que haga calor, la presentación será por la mañana.
por si (acaso)
indicative (or imperfect subjunctive)
Llévate un paraguas por si llueve.
de + simple infinitive
real / hypothetical condition
De ir, iría contigo. (= Si fuera…)
de + perfect infinitive
unreal condition in the past
De haberlo sabido, lo habría pedido. (= Si lo hubiera sabido…)
4. Como + subjunctive: the warning
In speech, “como” + SUBJUNCTIVE expresses a condition with a tone of warning or threat (often joking):
If you don’t keep me a seat, I’m going back with the books.
If you’re late, we’ll start without you.
If you lose it, I’ll kill you! (joking)

Don’t confuse it with causal “como” (+ indicative, at the start of the sentence): «Como no viniste, empezamos» (Because you didn’t come, we started) versus «Como no vengas, empezamos» (If you don’t come, we’ll start).

La presentación de Bucarest

The first copies of the Romanian edition arrived from the printer one Tuesday in April, in four cardboard boxes. The editor took them to Ecaterina’s home in person. Ecaterina opened the first box with scissors, very slowly, like someone opening a present she doesn’t dare look at. Inside, lined up like soldiers, were fifty books with a dark blue cover and, in the middle, the drawing of a green wooden shop sign: “Librăria de pe strada Huertas” (The Bookshop on Calle de las Huertas).

Ecaterina took out a copy and opened it at the first page. There were the two dedications, one below the other: Marta’s, in Spanish, and hers, in Romanian. “For A., who waited.” She ran her fingers over the letters, as if she wanted to make sure they were real. The editor, who had prepared a little speech, decided not to say anything.

The launch was set for 25 April, in the auditorium of the Instituto Cervantes. Marta had promised to come, provided someone could stay with her grandfather. Pilar, her mother, took a week’s leave from the hospital in Seville and moved into the flat on the calle del Prado. So, for the first time in two years, Marta was able to be away from her grandfather for more than a day. It was also the first time she had travelled to Romania.

Ana and Mihai went to pick her up at the airport with Rosa Elena, who was carrying a sign she had drawn herself: a tree with books on its branches and a single word, written with great effort, “Bienbenida”. Marta laughed when she saw the spelling mistake, crouched down, hugged the little girl and told her it was the most beautiful sign she had ever seen in her life, unless someone made her a better one, which she doubted.

That first afternoon, Ana showed her the city. They walked along Calea Victoriei, went into the Athenaeum, whose dome left Marta open-mouthed, and had a coffee in the courtyard of the Instituto Cervantes, where the launch was to be held. Marta confessed she had imagined Bucharest grey and sad, as in old films, and hadn’t expected so many flowers, so many lime trees or so many young people on the terraces. Ana replied that she had thought exactly the same the first time, and that was why she had stayed.

Marta stayed in Bucharest for four days, at Ana and Mihai’s. On the first day, Elena made her sarmale and explained, in a made-up Spanish mixed with Romanian and gestures, that you couldn’t leave Romania without having eaten sarmale at least three times. Marta ate six. On the second day, Mihai showed her Carmen’s frying pan hanging on the kitchen wall and made her a tortilla with onion which, according to Marta, was better than her mother’s, although she asked him never to tell her.

On the third day, which was a Sunday, Mihai offered to take her to Grandpa Gheorghe’s village, on condition that she didn’t talk to him about the weather, because Grandpa had very strong opinions about rain. They drove for two hours between green fields and villages with houses painted blue. Grandpa Gheorghe, who was ninety-five, was waiting for them on the bench by the gate, wearing his wool cap in spite of the heat.

Marta and Grandpa Gheorghe talked for an hour, with Mihai translating. He told her he remembered everything: the war, the friends of his youth, the photo of the three of them on the stone, the day Ion left without saying goodbye. Marta told him that her grandfather, on the other hand, was beginning to forget everything. Grandpa Gheorghe fell silent. Then he told her he didn’t know which was worse, remembering everything or remembering nothing, but that in both cases what mattered was that someone listened to you.

Before they left, Grandpa Gheorghe went into the house and came back with an unlabelled bottle of țuică. He gave it to Marta for her grandfather. He told her, through Mihai, that a small glass every Sunday wouldn’t do him any harm, provided the doctor didn’t find out. Marta promised she would give it to him secretly. Grandpa Gheorghe laughed for the first time that afternoon and told her she was now almost Romanian.

In the afternoons, Marta visited Ecaterina. They spent hours sitting in the kitchen, talking about Andrés. Ecaterina told her things Marta didn’t know: what her grandfather was like at forty, which books he recommended to shy customers, how he whistled while tidying the shelves. Marta, in return, told her about the last thirty years: Pilar’s wedding, her own birth, Sundays in the Retiro. It was as if each of them had half a book and they were putting it back together page by page.

On the day of the launch, the auditorium of the Cervantes was full an hour before it started. There were teachers, students, translators, journalists who this time had asked permission, readers who had followed the story online and, in the front row, the whole club. Aunt Viorica had promised not to film anything, unless Ecaterina gave her permission at the end. Costel had come straight from the car park, with the lorry parked in a nearby street.

The director of the Cervantes opened the event. Then the editor spoke, telling the story of the translation, without forgetting Domnul Dan’s comma, which made him blush in the front row. Then Marta spoke, in Spanish, with Ana translating. She told how the novel had been born: from conversations with her grandfather when he began to forget things and was afraid of forgetting everything. “He told me to write fast,” she explained, “unless I wanted to write a novel without an ending.”

Finally Ecaterina spoke. She stood up with the help of her stick, went to the microphone and, for a few seconds, said nothing. Then she opened the book at the last chapter and read in Romanian, slowly, the five pages that had taken her three nights to translate. Nobody moved. When she had finished, she closed the book and said a single sentence, first in Romanian and then in Spanish: “If someone had told me a year ago that this was going to happen, I wouldn’t have believed it. Had I known, I would have started translating much sooner.”

It was then that Marta’s phone rang. She looked at the screen and went pale. It was a video call from her mother, in Madrid. Marta hesitated for a second; then, with a gesture, she asked Ecaterina’s permission. Ecaterina nodded. Marta answered and turned the phone towards the audience. On the screen appeared Andrés’s face, in his armchair by the window, with Rayuela on his knees.

Pilar explained, her voice full of emotion, that her father had been asking all afternoon what time it was in Bucharest. That he had insisted on calling, unless the launch had already finished. Andrés looked at the screen. It took him a moment to understand where he was. Then he saw Ecaterina, standing by the microphone with the blue book in her hands, and he smiled that enormous smile that took twenty years off him.
“Is it translated already?” he asked.
“It’s translated,” Ecaterina answered him, in Spanish.
“Then you can come and fetch me now,” said Andrés. “As long as you bring a copy for me. And provided you haven’t taken another forty years.”

Two hundred people burst out laughing and crying at the same time. Aunt Viorica, with tears in her eyes, raised her phone and looked at Ecaterina pleadingly. Ecaterina, for once, gave her a nod of permission. Viorica filmed ten seconds, just ten: Andrés’s face on Marta’s phone, the whole hall applauding and Ecaterina holding the blue book up to the screen, like someone showing a trophy.

Viorica’s ten seconds became, within three days, the most watched video of her life: three million views. This time, however, nobody got angry. Under the video, Viorica had written a text that Ecaterina had corrected in person, word by word, with her red pencil: “Posted with permission. I’ve finally learnt to ask.” When Ecaterina read it, she said it was the best text Viorica had ever written, even though it was only eight words long.

After the launch, while Ecaterina was signing books, Costel came up to Ana and showed her a piece of paper. It was his boss’s permission, in writing, signed and stamped: Costel could carry in his lorry, on the May trip to Portugal, a hundred copies of the Romanian edition to the Madrid Book Fair, on condition that the Portuguese customer received his goods on time. Underneath, the boss had added by hand: “And bring me a signed one.”

That night, in Ana and Mihai’s kitchen, Marta and Ecaterina made a list of what they had to take to Madrid: the books, the notebook with the last chapter, which Ana was keeping, Rosa Elena’s drawing, a bottle of țuică from Grandpa Gheorghe and Carmen’s frying pan, which Mihai insisted on taking “in case an emergency tortilla is needed”. Nobody understood what emergency could call for a tortilla, but nobody dared to argue.

Before going to bed, Marta went out into the garden for a moment. She sat on the old tree stump, next to the little walnut tree, which already had new leaves. Ana saw her from the window. Marta was talking quietly on the phone with her grandfather. You couldn’t hear what she was saying. But at the end, Ana saw her smile and heard her say, a little louder, the sentence she would repeat a thousand times in the weeks that followed: “As long as you’re all right, Grandpa. As long as you’re all right.”
